concepts.def: The surface where one material ends and a different material begins, such as air and glass, air and water, or air and a brick wall. When a wave reaches a boundary it can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted.
When a wave meets the boundary between two different materials and is sent back into the material it came from. Reflection happens to all waves, not only to light, and not only at mirrors.

A construction line drawn at 90° to the surface at the point where the ray meets it. It is drawn as a dashed line and is the line from which the angles of incidence and reflection are always measured.

concepts.term: Angle of incidence and angle of reflection
concepts.def: The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal. The angle of reflection is the angle between the reflected ray and the normal. Neither is measured from the surface.
For a wave reflected at a surface, the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. The incident ray and the reflected ray lie on opposite sides of the normal.

A diagram showing the surface, the incident ray with an arrow towards the point of incidence, the dashed normal at 90° to the surface at that point, and the reflected ray with an arrow away from it, drawn so that the marked angle of reflection equals the marked angle of incidence.

When a wave crosses the boundary and carries on travelling through the second material. The wave travels at a different speed in the new material, so unless it meets the boundary along the normal it also changes direction.

When a wave is taken in by the material at the boundary and does not continue as a wave. The energy carried by the wave is transferred to the energy stores of the absorbing material, usually its thermal store, so the material warms up.

The change of direction of a transmitted wave at a boundary, caused by the change in the speed of the wave. Light entering glass or perspex from air slows down and bends towards the normal; on leaving into air it speeds up and bends away from the normal.

At a real boundary all three effects usually happen together in different proportions. A window reflects a faint image, transmits most of the light and absorbs a little; a black matt surface absorbs most of the light and warms up; a hard wall reflects sound to give an echo, while curtains and carpet absorb sound so echoes die away.

concepts.term: Reflection by different types of surface
concepts.def: In the required practical, a smooth shiny surface such as a plane mirror sends a narrow ray back as one clear reflected ray, while a rough surface such as white paper or crumpled foil scatters the light in many directions. Each individual ray still obeys the law of reflection; on a rough surface the normals point in many different directions.

Place the surface on a sheet of paper and draw round it. Shine a narrow ray from a ray box with a single slit at the surface. Mark the incident ray and the reflected ray with two dots each, well apart. Remove the surface, join the dots, draw the normal at 90° to the surface at the point of incidence, and measure the angles of incidence and reflection with a protractor. Repeat for different types of surface.

Place a transparent block on paper and draw round it. Shine a narrow ray into one face at a chosen angle of incidence and mark the ray going in and the ray coming out. Remove the block, join the marks to show the path inside, draw the normal at the point where the ray entered, and measure the angle of refraction. Repeat with blocks of different substances using the same angle of incidence each time, and compare how much each one bends the ray.

concepts.term: AT 4 and AT 8 in this practical
concepts.def: Both of these apparatus and techniques statements are about observing how waves interact with matter. They are met here by using a ray box or lamp with a single narrow slit, transparent blocks and different surfaces to observe how light is reflected and refracted, and by using a protractor and sharp pencil to record the angles accurately.

concepts.term: Working scientifically and maths skills in this practical
concepts.def: The investigation gives opportunities to identify and control variables, such as keeping the angle of incidence the same when different substances are compared, to measure angles to the nearest degree, to repeat readings and identify anomalies, and to plot and interpret a graph of angle of refraction against angle of incidence.

mcqs.q: A wave travelling through the air reaches the surface of a still pond. Which statement about reflection is correct?
options: No reflection happens here, because reflection needs a polished mirror surface.
Reflection happens only if the wave travels from the water into the air.
Some of the wave is reflected at the boundary between the air and the water.
Reflection happens only where the water surface is perfectly smooth.
mcqs.explain: Waves can be reflected at the boundary between two different materials; air and water are two different materials.

mcqs.q: A walker shouts towards a cliff face and hears an echo a moment later. What has happened to the sound wave?
options: It has been reflected at the boundary between the air and the rock.
It has been absorbed by the rock, which is why the sound returns later.
It has been transmitted through the rock and out of the other side.
It has been refracted as it entered the rock and then bent back out.
mcqs.explain: An echo is sound reflected back into the air at the boundary with a different material.

mcqs.q: A black matt surface is left in bright sunlight and becomes noticeably warm. Which statement best explains this?
options: Light is absorbed at the surface, so the energy carried by the wave is destroyed.
Light is absorbed at the surface and the energy is transferred to a thermal store.
Light is transmitted through the surface and carries its energy out the far side.
Light is reflected from the surface, and reflected waves always warm a material.
mcqs.explain: Absorption transfers the energy carried by the wave to the energy stores of the material, so it warms up.

mcqs.q: A ray of light travels from air into a thick glass block. Which statement is correct?
options: It is transmitted into the glass with its speed and its direction both unchanged.
It is absorbed at the boundary, so no light gets into the glass at all.
It is transmitted only if it meets the surface exactly along the normal.
It is transmitted into the glass, travelling at a different speed from before.
mcqs.explain: A transmitted wave carries on through the second material, and its speed there is different.

mcqs.q: In a ray diagram for reflection, the angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and which line?
options: The surface itself, at the point where the incident ray strikes the mirror.
The reflected ray, taking the whole angle between the two rays together.
The edge of the mirror, measured from the nearest end of the surface.
The normal, the line drawn at 90° to the surface at the point of incidence.
mcqs.explain: Both the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are measured from the normal.

mcqs.q: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror. The angle between the incident ray and the mirror surface is 30°. What is the angle of reflection?
mcqs.explain: The angle of incidence measured from the normal is 90° − 30° = 60°, and the angle of reflection equals it.

mcqs.q: A student draws a ray diagram of light reflecting from a plane mirror. Which feature shows that the diagram is correct?
options: The two rays are on opposite sides of the normal, with their angles to it equal.
The two rays are on the same side of the normal, with their angles to it equal.
The angles to the mirror surface are equal, so no normal needs to be drawn.
The reflected ray leaves at 90° to the mirror, whatever the incident ray does.
mcqs.explain: The law of reflection requires equal angles measured from the normal, with the rays on opposite sides of it.

mcqs.q: Thick curtains and a carpet are put into a bare room, and echoes in the room become much quieter. Which statement explains this?
options: The soft materials reflect the sound much better than the bare hard walls did.
The soft materials transmit all the sound straight out of the building.
The soft materials absorb more of the sound, so less of it is reflected back.
The soft materials slow the sound down so that it cannot get back again.
mcqs.explain: Soft, porous materials absorb sound energy at the boundary instead of returning it into the room.

mcqs.q: Standing in a lit room at night you can see the street outside a window and a faint reflection of yourself in it. What does this show?
options: Only one of reflection, transmission or absorption can happen at a boundary.
All of the light is transmitted, and the faint image comes from the air itself.
Reflection, transmission and absorption can all happen at the same boundary.
Glass reflects light only at night and transmits light only in the daytime.
mcqs.explain: The glass returns some light, lets most through and takes in a little, all at the one interface.

mcqs.q: In the required practical a narrow ray of light is shone first at a plane mirror and then at a sheet of white paper. What is seen?
options: The mirror gives one clear reflected ray; the paper scatters light in many directions.
The mirror gives one clear reflected ray; the paper reflects no light back at all.
Both give one clear reflected ray, but the paper reflects at a much larger angle.
Both scatter the light, because any surface breaks up a narrow ray of light.
mcqs.explain: A smooth surface keeps the reflected rays together; a rough surface has normals pointing many ways.

mcqs.q: In the refraction part of the practical, a narrow ray passes from air into a glass block at an angle to the normal. What happens as it enters?
options: It slows down and changes direction, bending away from the normal.
It slows down and changes direction, bending towards the normal.
It carries straight on without bending, whatever the angle of incidence.
It bends round the corner of the block rather than at the flat surface.
mcqs.explain: Light travels more slowly in glass than in air, and slowing at the boundary bends the ray towards the normal.

mcqs.q: The same ray reaches the far face of the glass block and passes back out into the air. What happens as it leaves?
options: It speeds up but bends towards the normal, as light always does.
It speeds up and bends away from the normal as it enters the air.
It carries on along the same line it followed inside the block.
It slows down and bends away from the normal as it enters the air.
mcqs.explain: The wave travels faster in air, and speeding up at the boundary bends the ray away from the normal.

mcqs.q: Why does a ray of light change direction as it passes from air into a perspex block?
options: The light bends around the edge of the block as it passes the corner.
The perspex absorbs some of the light, and absorbing it turns the beam.
The perspex is a solid, so it pushes the ray sideways as it goes in.
The light travels at a different speed in perspex than it does in air.
mcqs.explain: A change of wave speed at the boundary is the cause of the change of direction.

mcqs.q: In the practical a ray is aimed along the normal at the flat face of a glass block. What is observed?
options: The ray carries straight on without bending, though its speed does change.
The ray bends towards the normal, as it does at every angle of incidence.
The ray carries straight on and keeps exactly the same speed in the glass.
The ray is reflected straight back out along the path that it came in on.
mcqs.explain: At an angle of incidence of 0° there is no change of direction, but the wave still travels more slowly in the glass.

mcqs.q: AT 4 and AT 8 concern observing how waves interact with matter. Which technique makes the angles measured in this practical most reliable?
options: Use the widest and brightest beam available so that each ray is easy to see.
Use one narrow slit in the ray box and mark each ray with two dots set well apart.
Measure the angle inside the block by holding the protractor against the glass.
Measure the angles from the surface with a ruler rather than with a protractor.
mcqs.explain: A narrow ray has a definite path, and widely spaced dots make the pencil line and the angle accurate.

mcqs.q: A student investigates how much glass, perspex and water each bend a ray of light. Which variable must be controlled for the comparison to be valid?
options: The angle of incidence, changed for each substance so that more data is collected.
The width of the beam, made as wide as possible for each substance in turn.
The thickness of the block, changed so each ray travels a different distance.
The angle of incidence, kept the same for each of the three substances tested.
mcqs.explain: Only if the angle of incidence is fixed can any difference in bending be attributed to the substance.
